conflicts.entity: Canadian Camping Association (place of the founding meeting)
conflicts.description: TWO DOCUMENTED ACCOUNTS PUT THE CCA'S FOUNDING MEETING IN DIFFERENT CITIES. connections/institutional-lineage/canadian-camping-movement.md states, on the archival holdings, that 'In 1936, the Canadian Camping Association was founded at the Central Y.M.C.A. in Toronto on May 20, with Statten as first president.' Plewman -- a founder, present at the meeting, and the man who produced the association's first bulletin -- told Jay Haddad in a recorded interview on 15 August 1976: 'We did know there were camps in Quebec, so we invited them to a meeting and WE ALL MET IN OTTAWA and decided to have a Canadian Camping Association - and Taylor Statten was its first President.' The interview was printed in Canadian Camping Vol. 33 No. 6 (Winter 1982), pp. 4-5, after Plewman's death on 28 December 1981. Both are documented; the operator directive on oral history yielding to documents does not settle it, because Plewman's account is a documented publication of a recorded interview with a named participant, not undocumented oral tradition -- and because the two sources disagree about what a document says happened, which CLAUDE.md reserves for human review. NOT the same question as the competing 1936/1946/1949 founding DATES, which are tracked separately; Plewman's testimony agrees with 1936 and disagrees only about the city. Possible reconciliations to test before resolving: an organising meeting at Ottawa followed by a constituting meeting at the Toronto Central Y; Plewman recalling the wrong city at 86, forty years on; or the Toronto claim resting on a secondary source that assumed the association's Toronto address. The CCA fonds at Trent University hold the minutes.
conflicts.notes: Found by the full word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 140. HUMAN DECISION POINT under CLAUDE.md: two documented sources disagreeing with each other. Do not silently prefer either in any article; canadian-camping-movement.md now states both and points here. SECOND WITNESS AND A LEADING HYPOTHESIS (added 2026-09-04, issue 142): May Brown -- then director of the YWCA's Camp Oolahwan in Montreal, later CCA President 1965-67 -- said in a 1976 interview printed in Canadian Camping Vol. 34 No. 2 (Summer 1982), p. 4: 'I attended one of the first meetings on the CCA in Ottawa in the spring of 1947; I was really there as a Director of Camp Oolahwan which is the YWCA camp in Montreal.' She says 'one of the first meetings', not the founding, so this does not settle the conflict. But it makes a pattern of four separate items now pointing at Ottawa and at the later 1940s: (1) Plewman's 'we all met in Ottawa and decided to have a Canadian Camping Association'; (2) the Camp Stephens Alumni claim that Nelson McEwen 'founded the Canadian Camping Association in 1946' with Statten, which the article currently explains away as a possible 1946 reorganization; (3) the Newfoundland association's statement that the CCA 'was incorporated by Letters Patent at Ottawa November 5, 1949'; and (4) May Brown at Ottawa in spring 1947. LEADING RECONCILIATION TO TEST: that a body founded in 1936 out of the Ontario association's circle was constituted as a genuinely national, incorporated association at Ottawa across 1946-49, and that the memories, the Letters Patent and the competing founding dates describe one two-stage process rather than contradicting each other. This would reconcile nearly every rival origin claim the project holds. It is a hypothesis; the minutes at Trent (CCA/ACC fonds, Thomas J. Bata Library) are the document that decides it, and a Finding Aid for those archives exists and was circulated to every provincial association in 1981-82. THE ASSOCIATION'S OWN DATING (added 2026-09-04, issue 148): Bruno Morawetz's Archives Update in Canadian Camping Vol. 35 No. 3 (Autumn 1983), p. 13, reports that 'Cliff Labbett, Immediate Past President, is currently canvassing all the CCA Past Presidents for ideas to celebrate CCA's 50th Anniversary in 1986.' A fiftieth in 1986 dates the founding to 1936. This does NOT resolve c_029, which is about the CITY of the founding meeting and not its year -- Plewman and the archival holdings both say 1936. It is recorded here because it is the strongest evidence yet on the separately tracked 1936/1946/1949 DATE question: the association's immediate past president and its archives chairman, planning jointly in the year a professional archivist took charge of the fonds, acted on 1936. It supports the first stage of the two-stage hypothesis above and leaves the second (incorporation at Ottawa, 1946-49) untouched. THIRD CONFIRMATION IN CLEAN TYPE (added 2026-09-05, issue 152): the CCA's own Publications 1984-85 catalogue states the year outright in both languages -- 'The Canadian Camping Association was founded in 1936 as a non-profit organization' / 'L'Association des camps du Canada, creee en 1936'. Unlike the 50th-anniversary planning, this is an assertion of the founding year rather than an inference from an anniversary. It does NOT bear on this conflict, which is about the CITY of the founding meeting; Plewman and the archival holdings both say 1936. Recorded so that the separately tracked 1936/1946/1949 DATE question is not reopened on weaker evidence. A CCA PRESIDENT DATES IT TO c.1947 (added 2026-09-05, issue 156): Douglas G. McEwen, President, writing in Canadian Camping Autumn 1967 and reprinted Autumn 1985: 'For the first 20 years of its life the Canadian Camping Association's strength has lain in strong provincial associations.' Twenty years before 1967 is 1947. This is the sitting president describing the span of his own association's life, from a Manitoba-based executive, and it lands on the later side of the 1936/1946/1949 DATE question alongside Plewman's Ottawa recollection, the Camp Stephens claim that Nelson McEwen founded the CCA in 1946, May Brown's spring 1947 Ottawa meeting, and the Letters Patent of 5 November 1949. REMARKABLY, the SAME ISSUE carries the 1936 dating twice -- Adamson's 'In 1986 CCA/ACC will be celebrating fifty years' and the 1985-86 catalogue's 'founded in 1936' in both languages. The association printed both datings in one issue. That is the strongest support yet for the two-stage hypothesis, since it shows members operating on both datings at once. NOTE, not established and carrying no weight here: Douglas G. McEwen may be related to Nelson McEwen, Kanawana's director c.1927-1947, whom the Camp Stephens Alumni blog credits with founding the CCA in 1946. If that relationship holds, the two McEwens both dating the founding to the later 1940s stops being a coincidence and becomes a line of enquiry. THE FOUNDER'S DAUGHTER SAYS 1938 (added 2026-09-05, issue 158): in the CCA's own 50th anniversary issue, Adele Ebbs -- Taylor Statten's daughter, secretary to the founding circle and the person who kept its minutes from about 1935 -- was asked whether 1933 for the OCA and 1936 for the CCA sounded right. She said "'36 sounds early to me... '33 sounds right", and, on being reminded that her father helped F. M. Van Wagner form the QUEBEC association in 1937, said "well that is why I thought the Canadian Camping Association was not until... my impression was that it was 1938." The interviewer answered "We may be celebrating 50 years under false pretenses, so let's not upset that apple cart," and she conceded. THREE DATINGS NOW EXIST, ALL FROM INSIDE THE ASSOCIATION: 1936 (its 1980s literature and anniversaries), c.1947 (its president Douglas McEwen, writing in 1967), and 1938 (Adele Ebbs, 1986). Her reasoning -- a 1937 Quebec association, therefore a later national one -- is the kind a founding-circle secretary would have, and is again consistent with the two-stage hypothesis. ACTIONABLE: Ebbs says she began taking minutes of the pre-founding meetings of the six private directors (Edgar, Hamilton, Halliday, Chapman, Cochrane, Statten) 'sometime before I got married, and that was 1935'. THOSE MINUTES WOULD SETTLE IT. Ask Trent for them by that description. NOT NEW EVIDENCE, RECORDED SO IT IS NOT MISCOUNTED LATER (added 2026-09-05, issue 159): the Fall 1986 issue shows the 1936 dating being celebrated twice more -- a '50th Birthday Party for the Canadian Camping Association' held at the Moncton regional conference on the Saturday evening of 4 October 1986, cake provided by the New Brunswick Camping Association, and the '50th Anniversary Patrons' Fund' appeal over the names of Janet Adamson and Jack Pearse. Both are the SAME anniversary Adele Ebbs was told not to upset, not independent witnesses to 1936. Counted here as one continuing institutional assertion, not as two more sources. QUEBEC ITSELF DATED TO 1938, AND THE FOUNDING SIX RE-ATTACHED (added 2026-09-05, issue 160). (a) Ken Willis, writing as CCA/ACC Vice-President (Quebec Region) in Winter 1987: 'The organized camping movement in Quebec was born in 1938. Tony Shorgun... is already at work laying plans for the 50th Anniversary of this birth which, obviously, will be held next year.' What they jointly establish is that the 1937/1938 boundary was unclear to the participants -- a finding about the record, not grounds to prefer either. (b) THE SIX ARE THE OCA'S, NOT THE CCA'S. John Gilchrist, independently of Ebbs, named the same six -- Statten, Halliday, Cochrane, Hamilton, Chapman, Edgar -- and the interviewer identified what they formed: 'That was the Ontario Camping Association. Taylor Statten was the first President, in 1933.' So the supper club of private directors whose minutes Ebbs began keeping about 1935 is the ONTARIO founding circle. Whatever happened nationally in 1936, 1938 or 1947 is a separate act, and the six should no longer be cited as evidence about the national founding date. This narrows the question rather than answering it. (c) ACTIONABLE: if the Quebec 50th anniversary was held in 1988 it produced a programme or commemorative publication compiled by Tony Shorgun -- a name new to this project. Tracked in p_319. SHARPENED, NOT ADDED TO (2026-09-05, issue 164): the May Brown item above -- 'May Brown at one of its first meetings at Ottawa in the spring of 1947' -- now has provenance. This does NOT add a fifth item to the Ottawa cluster; it makes the existing one more specific and more credible, and it means a Quebec institution has a record of sending someone. Bruno Morawetz's Archives Update of Autumn 1983: 'Cliff Labbett, Immediate Past President, is currently canvassing all the CCA Past Presidents for ideas to celebrate CCA's 50th Anniversary in 1986.' The immediate past president and the archives chairman were jointly planning a fiftieth anniversary for 1986, which places the founding in 1936 -- the association acting on its own date, through the two officers most likely to have checked, in the year its archivist was appointed at Trent. This does NOT touch the Ottawa/Toronto question, which is what this conflict is about: Plewman said Ottawa, the archival holdings say the Central Y.M.C.A. in Toronto, and both agree on 1936. conflicts.description: TWO PRINTINGS OF THE SAME TRIBUTE GIVE DIFFERENT END DATES. The tribute read on Alta R. Kahn's appointment as the Quebec Camping Association English Section's first Honorary President, printed in Canadian Camping Vol. 26 No. 1 (Fall 1973), p. 12, gives her service as Executive Secretary of the Jewish Community Camps of Montreal -- Camp B'nai Brith, the Jewish Laurentian Fresh Air Camp and Wooden Acres -- as 1946 to 1949. Her obituary in Canadian Camping Vol. 36 No. 4 (Winter 1985), p. 2, signed by Frances Kelly and Robert Lazanik and clearly reworked from the 1973 text, gives the same service as 1946 to 1969. A single-digit typesetting or OCR slip (4 for 6, or 6 for 4) is the most economical explanation and neither reading is preferred here. Arguments each way: 1946-1969 fits the following sentence, 'During her years in this position, Mrs. Kahn instituted many new projects', and gives a 23-year tenure ending at a plausible retirement; 1946-1949 fits her preceding term as Executive Director of the Young Women's Hebrew Association (1936-1945) and her 1946 arrival in Quebec Camping Association work, and would leave her free for the QCA offices she held from 1958. The point is minor for Kanawana -- Kahn matters to this project as the co-chairman of the Quebec standards committee from 1959-60 -- but it is recorded because the no-silent-overwrite rule applies to small facts as well as large ones.
conflicts.notes: Found by the full word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 153. HUMAN DECISION POINT under CLAUDE.md only in the formal sense: two documented sources disagreeing. conflicts.entity: YMCA Camp Stephens, Lake of the Woods (year camping began) -- and, consequently, Kanawana's rank among Canada's oldest camps
conflicts.description: TWO DOCUMENTED DATES FROM INSIDE THE SAME INSTITUTION, NINETY YEARS APART. (a) 1891: Camp Stephens's own directors -- Grant Platts, Scott McGregor and Juliane Schaible of the Winnipeg YM-YWCA -- wrote in Canadian Camping Magazine Vol. 39 No. 1 (Summer 1987), p. 21: 'Y.M.-Y.W.C.A. Camp Stephens has been providing resident camping experiences for youth since 1891. It is one of the oldest resident camps in North America... Camp Stephens is looking forward to celebrating its 100th anniversary in 1991.' The same issue's 'What's In A Name?' (p. 27) adds: 'Originally known in 1891 as the Lake of the Woods Institute, the Y.M.C.A. Camp Stephens took its present name in 1896.' (b) JULY 1894: T. Duncan Patton -- a founder of Camp Kanawana -- records in his memoir that his first visit to the Lake of the Woods islands was July 1894, 'and from that date on camps were promoted and held annually,' the five islands passing to the Winnipeg YMCA in 1907. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND CAMP STEPHENS: this wiki asserted in three articles that Kanawana (1894) is 'Canada's second-oldest camp, after Big Cove (1889)'. If Camp Stephens has run since 1891, that ordinal is wrong. Taken with Big Cove's own director dating that camp to 1891 (Canadian Camping Magazine Vol. 38 No. 3, Winter 1987, p. 8) against the 1889 and 1890 already recorded in c_-adjacent notes, THREE of the four candidate dates for Canada's oldest camp now fall in 1889-1891, and Kanawana's 1894 follows all of them. A RECONCILIATION SUGGESTS ITSELF and is NOT adopted: the 1891 'Lake of the Woods Institute' may have been a men's conference-encampment rather than a children's resident camp, with youth camping beginning in 1894 as Patton describes. Neither source says so, and adopting it would be inventing the explanation that happens to preserve this project's own camp's ranking. ACTION TAKEN 2026-09-05: the ordinal ranking was WITHDRAWN from canadian-camping-movement.md, quebec-camp-landscape.md and timeline-overview.md, and replaced with 'Quebec's first residential summer camp and among the oldest in Canada', which every source supports. Kanawana's Quebec primacy is not in dispute. NEXT ACTION: ask the YMCA-YWCA of Winnipeg and the Manitoba provincial archives what the Lake of the Woods Institute of 1891 actually was, and whether the 1991 centenary produced a documented history; ask the Camping Association of Nova Scotia and the Halifax YMCA for a primary record of Big Cove's first season.
conflicts.notes:
Human decision point under the standing directive: two DOCUMENTED sources disagreeing with each other, not oral history against a document. No resolution is offered. The wiki text has been made safe in the meantime by dropping the claim that depends on the disagreement rather than by choosing a side.

[2026-09-05, continuity test] The operator asked whether 'oldest CONTINUOUSLY OPERATING camp' salvages the withdrawn ranking. Web research says no on the ordinal but yes on a better-defined claim. EVERY claimant has an interruption. Big Cove: its owner's own 165th anniversary yearbook says on p.8 that it is 'the oldest continuously running residential camp in Canada' and on p.28 that resident camping ceased after 1975 and resumed in 1980 -- four missed summers, in one publication, unreconciled. The gap was a closure for want of repairs (Byrne 1987) and a reopening, NOT a planned fallow period. Camp Stephens: its alumni association dates a wartime closure to 1917 ('the first closure since 1917'), where secondary summaries say 1918 -- disputed; Kanawana ran that season. Kanawana: 2020-21 lost to Quebec's prohibition. The pandemic separates nobody -- Big Cove also lost 2020-21 overnight and also kept its site in alternative use (cabin rentals, campground, leadership training), so 'we kept staff and site working' does NOT distinguish Kanawana. What does distinguish it is the longest unbroken run: 126 consecutive seasons 1894-2019, against ~102 for Stephens and ~87 for Big Cove, on any of Big Cove's candidate dates. This does not resolve c_031, which remains a founding-date conflict and a human decision point per the operator's instruction of 2026-09-05 to leave it as conflicting sources. See f_4739..f_4752.

conflicts.entity: The origin point of organized camping in Canada -- four competing printed claims, and Kanawana's place among them
conflicts.description: FOUR DISTINCT CLAIMS PRINTED IN THE SAME MAGAZINE WITHIN FIVE YEARS, NONE RECONCILED BY IT. (a) 1884, OTTAWA: a February 1955 item dates the first Canadian camp to an Ottawa YMCA camp at Golden Lake in 1884. (b) 1893/1908, OTTAWA YWCA: a December 1954 item cites an Ottawa YWCA minute of 1893 and dates Golden Lake camping to 1908 -- contradicting (a) about the same lake and city three months later. (c) 1889, CHANCE HARBOUR: "Ace" Milks, former director of Camp On-Da-Da-Waks at Golden Lake out of the Ottawa YMCA, writing about 1948 and printed February 1959: "The first Canadian Y.M.C.A. boys' camp, so far as we can discover, was organized by the Y.M.C.A. Committee of the Maritime Province and held at Chance Harbour, N.S., in the summer of 1889." Note that this is a hedged claim by a named individual retrieved from an Ontario Camping Association research file -- NOT, as f_2241 previously recorded it, a 1959 position of the Canadian Camping Association. Note also that Chance Harbour is in New Brunswick, not Nova Scotia, and that Big Cove -- the 1889 camp this project already carries with seven facts, and whose own director later dated it to 1891 -- is likewise in New Brunswick. Chance Harbour 1889 and Big Cove 1889 may be one camp under two descriptions or two separate camps; nothing in the record settles it. (d) 1905, NORTHWAY LODGE: Fannie Case's Northway Lodge, April 1955, claimed as "first girls' camp in Canada" -- a narrower claim that may not conflict with the others at all. WHY IT MATTERS: Kanawana's founding, dated July 1894 by T. Duncan Patton, follows (a) and (c) and precedes (d). Any ordinal claim this wiki makes about Kanawana's age depends on which of these is true, and none of them can currently be preferred on the evidence. ADDED 2026-09-05, A FIFTH CLAIM AND THE MOST AUTHORITATIVE: (e) 1890, TRURO, NOVA SCOTIA. "Towards Better Practices and Higher Standards," a statement commissioned by the National Committee on Youth Programme of the YMCA's of Canada and printed in Canadian Camping Vol. 13 No. 4 (June 1961), p. 180: "Canada's first organized camp was conducted by a YMCA Secretary at Truro, Nova Scotia, in 1890, and by the year 1905 there were thirteen different YMCA camps in Ontario and Quebec." Against claim (c) this is the same province, an adjacent year and a different town, and the source is the one institutionally closest to the event -- the YMCA of Canada's own national committee -- though it is no more contemporary than Milks. Truro is inland; Chance Harbour is coastal and in New Brunswick. Neither source cites the other. ADDED 2026-09-05, PARTICIPANT TESTIMONY ON THE OTTAWA DATE: C. F. Plewman -- "Formerly YMCA camp director, Founder of Camp Kilcoo," and himself a director for the Ottawa YMCA -- writes in Canadian Camping Vol. 17 No. 1 (December 1964): "When the Ottawa YMCA in 1893, and Camp Temagami in 1900, began taking older boys to camp, they were really breaking new ground." That is a participant's account, not a compiler's. It leaves claim (a), Ottawa 1884, standing alone against three independent 1893 sightings for the same city -- Plewman's, the Ottawa YWCA minute of 1893, and the associated Golden Lake material -- one of them from a man who ran the camp. The 1884 claim should now be treated as the weaker reading of the Ottawa question, though it is not thereby disproved and this record stays open.
conflicts.notes: Human decision point: documented sources disagreeing with each other. Related to c_031 (Camp Stephens 1891 vs 1894), which covers the other half of the same question. The two should probably be resolved together. The wiki has already been made safe by withdrawing the 'Canada's second-oldest camp' ordinal from three articles in favour of 'Quebec's first residential summer camp and among the oldest in Canada'; nothing further should be asserted until the underlying institutional records -- Maritime YMCA committee minutes, Ottawa YMCA and YWCA minute books -- are consulted directly. That statement also names two archival targets that would settle much of this: the Ontario and Quebec Boys' Work Committee's point-scored camp gradings from 1922, and the 1947 YMCA camping consultation papers. Extended 2026-09-05 with Plewman's December 1964 participant testimony, which shifts the weight of the Ottawa sub-question decisively toward 1893. That does not close the record: the 1884 claim is still a printed statement in the same magazine, and the Truro 1890 and Chance Harbour 1889 claims for the Maritimes are untouched by it.

conflicts.description: THREE DATES, ALL PRINTED IN CANADIAN CAMPING, NONE RECONCILED BY IT. (a) 1935: the unsigned Camp Tonakela report in Vol. 11 No. 4 (June 1959) dates the camp's inception to 1935; and, independently, J. H. Ebbs's signed obituary of Wallace Forgie in Vol. 20 No. 1 states "In 1935 he built Camp Tonakela near Madras, which was officially opened by Mr. and Mrs. Taylor Statten," crediting him with "thirty-two years of voluntary service," which from his death on 1 December 1967 counts back exactly to 1935. Ebbs was Adele Statten Ebbs's husband and so Forgie's nephew by marriage -- a close relative writing a signed memorial. (b) 1937: Adele Statten Ebbs, writing as Canadian Chairman of the Camp Tonakela Association after visiting the camp, states in Vol. 18 No. 2 (February 1966) "Camp Tonakela has been a demonstration of an overseas fellowship of campers and camping people since 1937"; and the camp's twenty-first birthday was celebrated on 21 February 1958, which implies February 1937. (c) JANUARY 1938: Vol. 10 No. 3 (April 1958) records Mr. and Mrs. Taylor Statten travelling to Madras to open the camp officially, citing The Madras Mail of 17 January 1938; J. Alex Edmison's Taylor Statten memorial in Vol. 14 No. 4 (June 1962) independently gives 1938 as the year Tonakela was established. THE LIKELIEST RECONCILIATION -- built 1935, camping from 1937, officially opened January 1938 -- fits every source, but it reconciles them rather than reporting any of them, and no source states it. An earlier pass in this project recommended resolving in favour of 1937 and marking 1935 superseded; that recommendation was too confident and is withdrawn, because 1935 has two independent documented supports of its own, one a signed memorial by a close relative.

conflicts.description: THREE DATES, ALL ATTESTED. (a) 1936: kb/facts.json records the CCA as founded in 1936 with Taylor Statten as its first president. (b) 1940: the CCA's own annual meeting of 1 March 1967 "marked the 27th Anniversary of the national association," per May Brown's report in Canadian Camping Vol. 19 No. 4 (June 1967), which implies 1940. (c) 1949: Mrs. J. Wesley Campbell's Centenary Journey statement in Vol. 17 No. 2 (February 1965) says "the Canadian Camping Association itself was incorporated in 1949," and the run's own first issue, February 1949, reports a new CCA constitution just accepted by the Secretary of State; W. E. Yard's 1966 tribute to Dais Gass adds that she chaired the meetings in Montreal, Toronto and Kingston that worked out "the first official charter of the Canadian Camping Association," which he first attended "early in 1949." A LIKELY RESOLUTION SUGGESTS ITSELF and is not adopted: that 1936 marks the founding of a Canadian section within the American Camping Association, 1940 a national organizing step, and 1949 the incorporation as an independent body -- consistent with Mary Edgar's statement that the CCA "no longer a section of the American Camping Association, held its first conference in Ottawa in May of 1947," and with Nan Vail's memory that the Gass years "were difficult times because the Executive was determined to have our Association become a National body separated from the American Camping Association." But no source states that sequence, and the 1940 figure is unexplained by it. Note also, from the same June 1967 issue, that Doug McEwen's profile credits "Mr. Nelson McEwen who, in conjunction with the late Mr. Taylor Statten, founded the Canadian Camping Association," serving as its first Secretary while National Boys' Work Secretary of the YMCA -- a co-founder this project's account does not name. EXTENDED (extraction pass, issue 92): Charles F. Plewman, who founded the magazine and was OCA president from the autumn of 1944, writes in Canadian Camping Vol. 24 No. 1 (Fall 1971): "Before very long, I think it was in 1946, the Canadian Camping Association was formed at a meeting held in the Chateau Laurier in Ottawa," adding that nearly all its members were representatives of the Ontario and Quebec associations, that no other province then had one, and that "for the moment it had no corporate existence." He also names "Miss Dais L. Gass, president of the C.C.A. in 1946" as author of the magazine's first editorial. This is a second, independent, first-hand source for a 1946 founding event, with a venue -- and it hedges the year, not the event. It does not overturn 1936, but it makes the 1946-reorganisation reading of the Camp Stephens claim about Nelson McEwen substantially more likely than an error, and turns the question into a checkable one: what happened at the Chateau Laurier in 1946. The CCA's own minutes should be in the OCA archives deposited at Trent in October 1970 (see p_348). EXTENDED AGAIN (extraction pass, issue 107): A DOCUMENTARY INCORPORATION DATE. The Newfoundland & Labrador Camping Association's entry in the January 1976 Directory Issue states that the CCA 'was incorporated by Letters Patent at Ottawa November 5, 1949.' That fits Plewman's own qualification exactly -- he put the founding meeting at the Chateau Laurier in 1946 and added that 'for the moment it had no corporate existence.' The three dates may therefore be three stages of one process rather than three rival claims: organising activity from 1936-37 (the Concordia holdings, and Van Wagner calling himself 'promoter and charter member' in 1937), a founding meeting in 1946, and incorporation on 5 November 1949. The QCA English Section took its own Federal Charter in 1949 as well, which suggests a single round of formalisation. The conflict stays open -- this places the dates in a sequence, it does not prove the sequence -- but the 1949 letters patent is the first documentary date in the record. EXTENDED AGAIN (extraction pass, issue 111): A FOUNDER SAYS 1936 IN HIS OWN PERSON. Charles Plewman, on being made an Honorary Member of the CCA: 'When the Canadian Camping Association was formed back in 1936, it was an act of faith, pure and simple. It was only a dream... because after all there were only two provinces in the whole of Canada that even had Camp Associations. In the thirty-eight years that have elapsed since that time, we have made that dream come true.' The internal arithmetic (1936 + 38 = 1974) places the address at the October 1974 annual meeting in Montreal; the February 1977 newsletter reprints it. So the SAME witness who dated a founding meeting to the Chateau Laurier in 1946 (issue 92) elsewhere dates the association's formation to 1936 -- which is a reason to read the two as stages rather than as rivals, and a reason not to treat Plewman as a witness for 1946 against 1936.

conflicts.description: THE OUTBREAK IS CERTAIN, THE YEAR IS OFF BY ONE. The wiki has carried it under one year without recording that the reporting convention makes the other possible.

conflicts.entity: Camp Stephens: continuous camp from 1891, or adult/family Bible camp until a first boys' camp in 1911
conflicts.description: THE CAMP'S OWN ANNIVERSARY SERVICE AGAINST THE CAMP'S OWN ANNIVERSARY. Camp Stephens dates itself to 1891 -- its current pages, its 125th anniversary in 2016, and two 1987 items in Canadian Camping written by its own directors (f_4665, f_4748). The script of its 125th Anniversary Chapel Service, read on the island on 31 July 2016, says something different about what was there: 'For the first twenty years of Stephens, it was predominantly an adult and family Bible camp', and 'It wasn't until 1911 that the first boys' camp was organized at Camp Stephens' (f_4840). The same script also has the Bible Institute founded in 1898, which its own 125-year occasion contradicts and which the Lake of the Woods Museum's 1893 site search sits against. THIS MATTERS TO KANAWANA'S OWN RECORD: the comparison in wiki/history/oldest-camp-question.md treats Camp Stephens as a rival resident camp from 1891-1893, and if boys' camping there began in 1911 the comparison is between two different kinds of institution for its first two decades. It is not resolved by preferring the more convenient reading. What would settle it: Winnipeg YMCA annual reports of the 1890s and 1900s, or the camp's own registers.
conflicts.notes: Raised 2026-09-05 while resolving c_061. HUMAN DECISION POINT in the proper sense: a commemorative script and an institution's own dating disagree about what the institution WAS, and neither is a document from the period.
